description: Adapted from ecological systems theory, the adaptive cycles framework describes learning as moving through four non-linear phases — problematization, reorganization, growth, and conservation — each of which opens the learner to different kinds of support.
title: Adaptive Cycles Framework

title: Adaptive expertise in teaching: adaptivity as a key characteristic of effective teaching, with identifiable core practices

description: Adolescent brain development is marked by a maturational mismatch — the limbic system's reward and emotion circuitry matures years before the prefrontal cortex's executive-control circuitry — that helps explain adolescent risk-taking, emotional intensity, and sensitivity to social reward.
title: Adolescent Brain Development

description: The review presents an emergent neurobiological model in which \"the brain undergoes dynamic changes throughout adolescence\" and structural and behavioral changes interact.
title: Adolescence as a neurobiological 'reconstruction zone' — a sensitive period in which experiential input shapes executive function and social cognition

description: Adolescent peer relationships are organized through overlapping structures — small, interaction-based cliques and larger, reputation-based crowds — with individual acceptance further describable through sociometric status categories, and peer influence operating partly through homophily and partly through active peer contagion.
title: Adolescent Peer Group Structure

description: ADSD is a proposed metric that quantifies sentiment bias by measuring the divergence between the sentiment-score distributions a model produces for original posts and for gender-counterfactual posts.
title: Absolute distributional sentiment divergence (ADSD) as a distribution-level fairness metric for generated replies

description: The guide organizes the adult learning market around two customer segments.
title: Two-segment customer taxonomy for the adult learning ed-tech market: learning providers as primary segment, independent learners as secondary segment

description: The digest presents a neurolinguistic account, citing Walsh and Diller (1978), that replaces the 1960s critical-period hypothesis.
title: Neurolinguistic account of adults' superior language learning capabilities
